name: Ontario
summary_text: Ontario stands under the national framework of Canada, one of the safer large destinations for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly across the country, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction; legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, and federal identity documents can carry an X marker.  The provincial guarantee is written into statute. The Ontario Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on those grounds is the official provincial statement of the protections a trans person holds. It states that people are protected from discrimination and harassment on these grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The policy defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender, giving an explicit official basis for lodging a discrimination complaint.  Violence risk is measurable but the data does not isolate trans experience. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents in Canada in 2024, 1% more than in 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000 people. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting levels are shaped by awareness and community trust. National crime releases break out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is not established by this dataset; Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation, has published a 2024 analysis of the same police-reported data covering both sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations.

name: Prince Edward Island
summary_text: Prince Edward Island stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply in Prince Edward Island as they do across the country.  Legal gender recognition in Prince Edward Island carries no surgery requirement. A 2016 amendment to the Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration of the gender the applicant identifies with, supported by a letter from a doctor. The regime has operated on that basis ever since. An adult born in the province may apply if resident there for at least three months; the application requires completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, signed before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.  Provincial photo ID can carry a non-binary or undisclosed marker. Since 4 December 2018 Islanders completing a driver's licence at Access PEI locations may select 'gender not listed', shown on the licence as X, or 'prefer not to say', shown as a blank, alongside male and female. The Government of Prince Edward Island stated that the province was the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank option.  National police-reported hate-crime data gives no Prince Edward Island figure. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000 population, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province.
